translationRepairs: Also because in the second year of Yuanfu an immortal crane at the temple of Lord Wuyi welcomed an edict, and in the second year of Zhenghe, when ministers were feasted at Yanfu Palace, a flock of cranes came from the northwest and circled above Rui Mo Hall, and flying cranes repeatedly appeared when the Dasheng music was performed, an edict ordered the creation of the Auspicious Crane flag.

Also because in the second year of Yuanfu an immortal crane at the temple of Lord Wuyi welcomed an edict, and in the second year of Zhenghe, when ministers were feasted at Yanfu Palace, a flock of cranes came from the northwest and circled above Ruimo Hall, and flying cranes repeatedly appeared when the Dasheng music was performed, an edict ordered the creation of the Auspicious Crane flag.
睿謨殿 is the proper hall name Ruimo; splitting it as Rui Mo obscures the unitary toponym.

In the eighth year, Vice Minister of Rites Zhang Bangchang memorialized: "In the time of Emperor Taizu, sweet dew fell at Jiangling for ten days, auspicious wheat with six ears appeared at Puyang, a golden parrot was captured on the Long Plateau, three jade rabbits were obtained at Yun Prefecture, tame elephants arrived when the Five Ridges were pacified, and a white deer appeared when the Qiong tribes submitted. All of these were ordered made into flags and displayed.

In the eighth year of Zhenghe, Vice Minister of Rites Zhang Bangchang memorialized: "In the time of Emperor Taizu, sweet dew fell at Jiangling for ten days, auspicious wheat with six ears appeared at Puyang, a golden parrot was captured on the Long Plateau, three jade rabbits were obtained at Yun Prefecture, tame elephants arrived when the Five Ridges were pacified, and a white deer appeared when the tribes of Qiongguan submitted. All of these were ordered made into flags and displayed.
Bare 八年 continues the Zhenghe frame and should be dated, and 瓊管 is the Qiongguan circuit, but 族 remains 'tribes'; the proposal wrongly drops 族 by making the administration itself submit.
Master Zheng said: "Liu means fixing yak tails at the pole head.
Master Zheng said: "Rui means fixing yak tails at the pole head.
鄭氏 glosses 緌 (rui), the Xia banner tassel term from the prior citation; Liu confuses it with 旒.
Master Zheng said: "Liu means fixing yak tails at the pole head.
Master Zheng said: "Rui means fixing yak tails at the pole head.
The literal likewise must gloss 緌 as Rui, not Liu.
This guard staff is nearest the imperial carriage and therefore corresponds to the elephant, taking the center to guide the four directions and spread great light."
This guard staff is nearest the imperial carriage and therefore corresponds to the symbolic image, taking the center to guide the four directions and spread great light."
應象 means correspondence to the symbolic image of centrality after 黃，中央之色, not an elephant.
This guard staff is nearest the imperial carriage, and therefore corresponds to the elephant, taking the center to guide and reach the four directions, containing and spreading great light."
This guard staff is nearest the imperial carriage, and therefore corresponds to the symbolic image, taking the center to guide and reach the four directions, containing and spreading great light."
In the literal too, 應象 is symbolic correspondence, not elephant.

In the seventh year of Yuanyou, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices reported: The Kaiyuan Rites prescribe an octagonal purple umbrella for the grand procession and four-cornered green umbrellas for princes, dukes, and those below.

In the seventh year of Yuanyou under Emperor Zhezong, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices reported: The Kaiyuan Rites prescribe an octagonal purple umbrella for the grand procession and four-cornered green umbrellas for princes, dukes, and those below.
哲宗元祐七年 explicitly names Emperor Zhezong; the idiomatic must not omit 哲宗.
The Jin replaced it with wood, also called the "elephant sword," taking the meaning of ornate decoration.
The Jin replaced it with wood, also called the "imitative sword," taking the meaning of ornate decoration.
晉以木代之，亦曰象劍 takes 象 as likeness of the wooden substitute, explained as ornate decoration, not an elephant.
The Jin replaced it with wood, also called the "elephant sword," taking the meaning of ornate decoration.
The Jin replaced it with wood, also called the "imitative sword," taking the meaning of ornate decoration.
The literal must likewise render 象劍 as the imitative wooden sword, not an elephant sword.
In the seventh year of Yuanyou, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices reported: "For ceremonial horses, according to the Imperial Escort Diagram, saddle cloth was formerly also applied.

In the seventh year of Yuanyou under Emperor Zhezong, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices reported: "For ceremonial horses, according to the Imperial Escort Diagram, saddle cloth was formerly also applied.
哲宗元祐七年 again names Emperor Zhezong; the idiomatic omission is a real error.
Sheep-carriage attendants wore hanging-ear topknots, green headcloths, green embroidered large-sleeve shirts, trousers, waist sashes, and green ear-shoes.
Sheep-carriage boys wore hanging-ear topknots, green headcloths, green embroidered large-sleeve shirts, trousers, waist sashes, and green ear-shoes.
駕羊車童子 specifies boys (童子), not generic attendants.
Sheep-carriage attendants wore hanging-ear topknots, green headcloths, green embroidered large-sleeve shirts, trousers, waist sashes, and green ear-shoes.
Sheep-carriage boys wore hanging-ear topknots, green headcloths, green embroidered large-sleeve shirts, trousers, waist sashes, and green ear-shoes.
The literal likewise must render 童子 as boys, not attendants.

In the fourth year of Jianlong, Fan Zhi proposed: According to the Kaiyuan Rites, when military officers stood attendance at the great guard formation, they added teng-snake doublets like sleeves without a body to cover the upper arms, sewn under the armpit.

In the fourth year of Jianlong under Emperor Taizu, Fan Zhi proposed: According to the Kaiyuan Rites, when military officers stood attendance at the great guard formation, they added teng-snake doublets like sleeves without a body to cover the upper arms, sewn under the armpit.
太祖建隆四年 names Emperor Taizu as the reign context; the idiomatic must not drop 太祖.
